p: The writer holds that God punishes people through the very things they sin by, here the animals Egypt worshiped.
b: The chapter picks up the rule of 11:16, "what a person sins with, he is punished with" (see also 15:18–19): Egypt honored animals as gods, so animals became its punishment. This is the book's rule of fitting punishment, sometimes called "measure for measure." Jewish readers know the rule from later rabbinic teaching; Christian readers hear it in Paul's "God handed them over" in Romans 1. Historians note that animal cults really were popular in Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt, so the charge was not abstract for Jews living in Alexandria. From here to 19:21 the book sets Egypt's plagues beside Israel's blessings, one pair at a time.

p: Numbers tells the quail story as a punishment. Wisdom tells only the gift.
b: Goes beyond and selects: in Exodus 16:13 quail come in the evening before the first manna, with no judgment. In Numbers 11 the people's craving brings quail and then a plague: "The meat was still between their teeth, not yet chewed up, when the LORD's anger burned against the people" (Numbers 11:33). Wisdom keeps the craving ("to satisfy their craving") but leaves out the plague, because its point here is contrast: the Egyptians lost their appetite at the sight of vermin, Israel got a new food. The book's habit is to soften Israel's failures in the wilderness, and it comes back to the quail in 19:11–12.

p: Verses 5–14 retell Numbers 21:4–9, the burning snakes and the bronze snake on the pole.
b: In Numbers the people complain about the manna ("we are sick of this flimsy food!" Numbers 21:5), and "the LORD sent the burning snakes among the people" (Numbers 21:6). Wisdom does not mention the complaint. It calls the bites a short warning (16:6) and stresses that the anger "did not last to the end." The writer has to face an awkward fact: in this contrast Israel too was bitten. He answers that Egypt's plague was fatal and final (16:9), Israel's was brief and healing came with it.

t: Not a magic object but a reminder
p: The Greek σύμβολον, "token," appears nowhere else in Swete's Greek Old Testament.
b: The Greek of Numbers 21:8–9 says Moses set the snake ἐπὶ σημείου, "on a sign" or "standard." Wisdom chooses a rarer word, σύμβολον, a token or pledge that points beyond itself, and says what it pointed to: "to remind them of what your law commands." The bronze snake becomes a teaching device, not a charm. A search of Swete's whole Septuagint finds σύμβολον only here. The word later became important in Christian Greek (a creed is a "symbol"), but Wisdom uses it in its plain sense of a token.

a: The one who turned to it
t: Turned toward it, or turned back?
p: The Greek ἐπιστραφείς can mean turning to look, or turning back to God.
b: The participle ἐπιστραφείς is the ordinary Septuagint verb for turning around, and also for returning to God in repentance. Numbers 21:9 only says the bitten man "would look at the bronze snake and live." Wisdom's word lets both senses ring: the man turned toward the pole, and in doing so turned to God. The next line makes the second sense the point.
orig: ὁ ἐπιστραφείς (ho epistrapheis), 'the one who turned'

a: but by you, the Savior of all
t: Who healed: the snake or God?
p: Wisdom, the Mishnah and the Gospel of John all ask what really saved the bitten Israelites.
b: Jewish reading. The Mishnah asks the same question: "Did the serpent kill, or did the serpent preserve life?" Its answer is that people were healed when they looked upward and gave their hearts to their Father in heaven (Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 3:8). Wisdom gives the same answer more than a century earlier. Both guard against magic, the danger that ended with Hezekiah, who "crushed to pieces the bronze snake Moses had made, because up to those days the Israelites had been burning incense to it" (2 Kings 18:4). Christian reading. John 3:14–15 makes the lifted snake a picture of the Son of Man lifted up, and many Christians read Wisdom's "Savior of all" alongside it. Wisdom itself speaks of God, not of a coming savior.

a: The bites of locusts and flies killed them
p: Exodus never says the locusts or the flies killed anyone. Wisdom adds it.
b: Goes beyond: Exodus 8:24 says the swarm "brought the land to ruin," and in Exodus 10:15 the locusts "ate every plant of the land," but neither account reports deaths. Wisdom adds them, so that the contrast with the bitten Israelites who lived (16:10) is complete. The writer is not inventing for its own sake: he reads the plague stories as a pattern of judgment and mercy and fills in what the pattern needs. Most readers treat such details as the book's interpretation rather than as extra history.

p: Here ψυχή means a person's life, as it often does in Greek.
b: The site keeps "soul" for ψυχή all through Wisdom, because the book's teaching about the soul (3:1; 9:15) matters. But in this verse the sense is simply physical life: no remedy could keep them alive. The same is true of the "soul that has been taken" in 16:14, where death is meant.

p: Not medicine but God's word cured them. The line echoes Psalm 107:20.
b: Wisdom says the bitten were cured not by "herb or soothing ointment" but by God's λόγος, "word." The thought is the psalm's: "He sent his word to heal them" (Psalm 107:20). In this book God's word is God acting, the same word that in 18:15 comes down as a warrior. The site renders λόγος "word" with a small letter here and in 18:15, so that the Plain does not decide the Christian question in advance; see the note at 18:15. Ancient medicine used herbs and poultices, and the line does not condemn them (Sirach 38 praises doctors); it says where healing comes from.
orig: ὁ σός, Κύριε, λόγος (ho sos, Kyrie, logos), 'your word, Lord'

t: Death and life in God's hand
p: "You bring down ... and you bring back up" quotes the faith of Hannah's song and Moses' song.
b: The verse echoes two old confessions: "The LORD kills and makes alive; / he takes down to Sheol, and he brings up" (1 Samuel 2:6), and "I kill, and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). Hades is the Greek word for Sheol, the place of the dead. "The gates of Hades" also appear in Hezekiah's psalm (Isaiah 38:10, there "the gates of Sheol") and in Jesus' promise that "the gates of Hades will not be stronger than" his church (Matthew 16:18). In Wisdom the point is God's power to rescue from the edge of death, as with the bitten Israelites.

a: The ungodly refused to know you
t: Pharaoh: "I do not know the LORD"
p: The charge answers Pharaoh's own words in Exodus 5:2.
b: At the start of the Exodus Pharaoh says, "I do not know the LORD" (Exodus 5:2), and the Greek there uses the same verb, οἶδα, "know," that Wisdom uses here. The plagues are God's answer: again and again Exodus says they come so that Pharaoh and Egypt will know the LORD: "Then you will know that I am the LORD" (Exodus 8:22; compare Exodus 14:4). Wisdom says the Egyptians "refused" or "denied" knowing God, so their ignorance was chosen, the same charge it brought against the worship of nature in 13:1–9.

a: the world itself fights for the righteous
p: A key idea of chapters 16–19: the created world takes the side of the righteous.
b: The hail of Exodus 9:24 had fire "catching and flaring in the middle of the hail." Wisdom finds the most amazing thing in this: fire burning in water. Its explanation is a principle stated in 16:24 and 19:6: creation serves its Maker, tightening against the wicked and loosening for the righteous. Greek readers would hear Stoic language about a single ordered κόσμος, but Wisdom gives the order a will, God's. The same idea appears in 5:17–20, where God arms creation against his enemies.
orig: ὑπέρμαχος γὰρ ὁ κόσμος ἐστὶν δικαίων (hypermachos gar ho kosmos estin dikaiōn)

t: Bread of the mighty, bread of angels
p: The Hebrew of Psalm 78:25 says "bread of the mighty ones"; the Greek says "bread of angels."
b: Psalm 78:25 in Hebrew reads lechem abbirim, which this site renders "Each one ate the bread of the mighty ones." The Septuagint translated it ἄρτον ἀγγέλων, "bread of angels" (Psalm 77:25 in its numbering), and Wisdom follows the Greek. The Talmud records the same debate among rabbis: Rabbi Akiva said "bread of the mighty" is bread the ministering angels eat; Rabbi Ishmael objected that angels do not eat, citing Moses on the mountain, who ate no bread (Deuteronomy 9:9), and read it as bread wholly absorbed by the body (Yoma 75b). The Latin panis angelorum later entered Christian hymns of the Eucharist.

p: Exodus, the Psalms and John 6 all call the manna bread from heaven.
b: God says, "I am about to make bread fall like rain from the sky for you" (Exodus 16:4), and the psalms sing "he gave them their fill of bread from heaven" (Psalm 105:40). In John 6 the crowd quotes the line to Jesus, "Bread from heaven he gave them to eat" (John 6:31), and Jesus answers that "it is my Father who gives you the bread out of heaven, the true bread" (John 6:32). Wisdom's praise of the manna is one of the clearest Jewish examples of what the crowd in John 6 had in mind. Paul calls it "the same spiritual food" (1 Corinthians 10:3).

a: with the power to give every kind of pleasure
p: The Latin of this line is the response sung after the Tantum ergo in Catholic worship of the Eucharist.
b: At Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament in the Roman Rite, the hymn Tantum ergo is followed by a versicle and response: "You have given them bread from heaven" and "Having within it all sweetness" (Latin Omne delectamentum in se habentem), taken from this verse. Catholics apply Wisdom's praise of the manna to the Eucharist, which they believe is the true bread from heaven that the manna foreshadowed (John 6:32–51). Jewish readers read the verse of the manna itself. The Latin follows the reading of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (see the variant on this verse).

a: to be in tune with every taste
t: The manna tasted like whatever you wanted
p: Wisdom and the Talmud share a tradition that the manna took on every flavor.
b: Exodus 16:31 says manna "tasted like a honey wafer" and Numbers 11:8 says "like a cake made with rich oil." Jewish teachers resolved the difference by saying it tasted of everything. In the Talmud, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi agree that "they tasted the flavor of all types of food in the manna," and Rabbi Abbahu compares it to a mother's milk, which changes taste with what she eats (Yoma 75a). Wisdom 16:21 says the same centuries earlier: it "was changed into whatever each one wished." The Greek ἁρμόνιον is a musical word, "in harmony with."
orig: πρὸς πᾶσαν ἁρμόνιον γεῦσιν (pros pasan harmonion geusin)

p: The Greek ὑπόστασις can mean the food God provided, or God's own nature showing itself.
b: Ὑπόστασις means what stands under or supports: so "provision, sustenance" (the KJV and Douay have "thy sustenance"), but also "substance, real being." Some readers take the line as "your nature showed your sweetness," that is, the manna revealed what God is like. The word later became a technical term of Christian theology, and Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son "the exact stamp of his being" (ὑποστάσεως). Here the first, simpler sense fits the context of food best, so the Plain says "provision."

p: "Snow and ice" is the manna, which looked like frost but could be cooked.
b: Exodus says the manna was "thin like frost on the ground" (Exodus 16:14; the Greek has πάγος, "frost"), and Numbers says the people "boiled it in a pot and made it into cakes" (Numbers 11:8). So the writer notices a paradox: this "snow" stood up to fire in the oven, yet it "melted" when the sun grew warm (Exodus 16:21). In Egypt fire had burned inside hail; in the wilderness fire spared the ice-like manna. Both, he says, show that the elements obey God (16:24). He returns to the image in 19:21.

p: The verbs are words for tightening and slackening a string or rope.
b: Ἐπιτείνω means to stretch tight, as a musician tightens a string to raise its pitch; ἀνίημι means to let it go slack. Creation is pictured as an instrument in God's hands, made tense against the unrighteous and relaxed in kindness toward those who trust him. The same musical picture closes the book in 19:18, where the elements are re-tuned like the notes of a harp. Greek philosophers sometimes spoke of the world's "tension"; Wisdom makes the tension God's choice.
orig: ἐπιτείνεται ... ἀνίεται (epiteinetai ... anietai), 'is tightened ... is slackened'

a: a human being is not fed by crops springing up
p: The verse restates Deuteronomy 8:3, the line Jesus quoted when he was tested.
b: Moses told Israel the manna came "to teach you that people do not live by bread alone. People live by everything that comes out of the LORD's mouth" (Deuteronomy 8:3). Wisdom draws the same lesson in its own words: not the harvest but God's ῥῆμα, his spoken "word," keeps believers alive. Jesus answers the tempter with the Deuteronomy line: "People will not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes out of God's mouth" (Matthew 4:4). Wisdom shows how Jews of the time were already reading the manna as a lesson about God's word.

a: be up ahead of the sun to thank you
p: The melting manna becomes a lesson: pray at dawn, before the sun is up.
b: The manna had to be gathered early, because "when the sun grew warm, it melted" (Exodus 16:21). Wisdom turns this into a rule of prayer: thank God before the sun rises. Jewish practice set the morning Shema from first light, to be finished by sunrise (Mishnah Berakhot 1:2), and Josephus says the Essenes spoke no ordinary word before sunrise but said their ancestral prayers first (Jewish War 2.128). Christians kept dawn prayer in the morning office. Wisdom's line is one of the earliest Jewish witnesses to the custom.

t: Three days of darkness, greatly enlarged
p: Exodus gives the darkness three verses. Wisdom gives it a whole chapter, with phantoms and terror.
b: Goes beyond: Exodus 10:21–23 says only that "darkness upon darkness lay over all the land of Egypt for three days," that no one could see his brother or get up, and that "for all the Israelites there was light in their homes." Wisdom 17 adds ghosts, noises, the failure of magic, and fear that kills. It does not claim new facts so much as explain: the darkness was inward as well as outward (17:21), a punishment fitted to people who thought their "secret sins would go unseen." Catholic and Orthodox readers take such retelling as inspired interpretation; Protestant and Jewish readers as a vivid ancient sermon on Exodus.

p: The phrase comes from Exodus 19:6 and is applied to the church in 1 Peter 2:9.
b: At Sinai God tells Israel "you will be for me a kingdom of priests, a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6). Wisdom calls the slaves in Egypt by that title even before Sinai, because to the writer Israel's calling is already settled (see 18:4). First Peter gives the same title to believers in Jesus: "you are a chosen family, a royal priesthood, a holy nation" (1 Peter 2:9). How Israel's titles relate to the church is a question Christians answer in different ways; see the topic on the church and Israel.

p: Πρόνοια, "providence," was a key word of Greek philosophy. Wisdom uses it of God.
b: Pronoia means "forethought," the care that plans ahead. Stoic and Platonic writers used it of the divine reason that runs the world. In Swete's Greek Old Testament it occurs in Wisdom (14:3; 17:2), Daniel 6:18, and 2, 3 and 4 Maccabees, all late and Greek-flavored books. Wisdom gives the word a biblical meaning: the personal care of the God of Israel. The Egyptians are "exiles" from it, shut out by their own choice, while Israel walks in it.

a: The tricks of their magic arts
p: Pharaoh's magicians copied the first plagues but could not copy the gnats.
b: In Exodus the magicians "did the same with their spells" (Exodus 7:11; 8:7), until the gnats, when "they could not" and confessed, "It is the finger of God" (Exodus 8:18–19). Wisdom says their failure became public shame in the darkness: those who sold cures for fear were the most afraid (17:8). Later Jewish tradition named two of them Jannes and Jambres, and 2 Timothy 3:8 uses the names: "Jannes and Jambres stood against Moses." Egypt's priests were famous in the Greek world for magic, which gave the verse a sharp edge in Alexandria.

p: This is the only place the Greek Old Testament uses συνείδησις for the conscience that accuses.
b: Συνείδησις means "knowing with oneself," the inner witness to one's own wrong. In all of Swete's Septuagint the noun appears only here and in Ecclesiastes 10:20, where it means one's private thoughts ("do not curse the king even in your thoughts"). So Wisdom 17:11 is the first clear use in the Greek Bible of the moral conscience that Paul makes so important: "Their conscience testifies with it" (Romans 2:15). The verse also gives a psychology of guilt: a condemned wickedness is cowardly and always imagines the worst.

a: For fear is nothing but reason's help betrayed
p: Wisdom stops the story to define fear, in the manner of Greek moral philosophy.
b: Greek moralists, above all the Stoics, liked short definitions of the passions, and taught that reason (λογισμός) is the help the mind has against them. Wisdom 17:12–13 uses that style: fear is the surrender of reason's defenses, and the less a person knows, the worse the unknown cause seems. The idea is close to 4 Maccabees, a later Jewish book whose whole theme is reason, devoted to God, ruling the passions. The writer shows he can speak to educated Greeks in their own terms while retelling Exodus.

p: Ἀδύνατος can mean "powerless" or "unbearable." Wisdom uses it twice in one line.
b: The Greek calls both the night and Hades ἀδύνατος. Its basic sense is "powerless, without strength," which makes a point: the darkness and the underworld it came from had no real power; only the Egyptians' guilt made them terrible (17:11). But the word can also mean "impossible" or "unbearable," and the KJV took it that way ("intolerable," "inevitable"). The Plain keeps the basic sense.
orig: τὴν ἀδύνατον ὄντως νύκτα ... ἐξ ἀδυνάτου ᾅδου (tēn adynaton ontōs nykta ... ex adynatou hadou)

p: The darkness itself was the jail: no walls, no chains, yet no one could move.
b: Exodus 10:23 says "no one got up from where he was for three days." Wisdom pictures this as a prison with no iron (ἀσίδηρος εἱρκτή) and "one chain of darkness" binding farmer, shepherd and laborer alike (17:17–18). The image matches the book's view that sin imprisons from within. Second Peter 2:4 and Jude 1:6 use the language of chains and darkness for fallen angels kept for judgment.

a: a picture of the darkness that was going to take them in
t: Darkness now and darkness to come
p: The plague of darkness is a preview of a darker end. Readers differ on what end is meant.
b: Wisdom calls the night an εἰκών, an image, of the darkness that would receive them. Some read this of death and Hades, which the Egyptian army met at the sea (19:5). Others, both Jewish and Christian, read it of judgment after death, as in the book's earlier chapters on the end of the ungodly (4:19; 5:1–14). Christian readers hear Jesus' words about "the darkness outside" (Matthew 8:12) and the "gloom of darkness" kept for false teachers (Jude 1:13). The last line adds a sharp point: their own guilt weighed on them more than the dark.

p: Wisdom calls Israel οἱ ὅσιοι, "the holy ones" or "the devout," not angels.
b: Ὅσιος means devout, faithful to God. In 18:1, 5 and 9 the writer uses it for the Israelites in Egypt, as the Greek Psalms often use it for the faithful. The Plain says "holy ones" to keep the link between the verses. In 18:9 another word, ἅγιοι, also appears; it is rendered "the holy people" there, not "the saints," since "saints" in English suggests Christians or canonized holy people.

p: Wisdom moves straight from the darkness in Egypt to the pillar of fire on the road out.
b: Exodus 13:21 says the LORD went before them "by night in a pillar of fire to light their way." Wisdom sets this beside the plague of darkness: Egypt had a night no fire could light, Israel had a fire that lit the night. It calls the pillar "a sun that did no harm," perhaps thinking of Psalm 121:6 or Isaiah 49:10, where the sun does not strike God's people. Revelation 7:16 promises the same: "the sun will not fall on them." In 10:17 the book had already said that Wisdom was "a flame of starlight at night."

t: Israel, carrier of the law's light
p: Israel was kept alive so that the light of the law would reach the whole world.
b: Here Wisdom states Israel's mission plainly: the Egyptians who jailed Israel tried to shut up the people "through whom the world was going to receive the law's imperishable light." The thought echoes Isaiah's servant, "a light to the nations" (Isaiah 42:6), and Proverbs, where "teaching is light" (Proverbs 6:23). It was a bold claim for Jews in Alexandria, where Greek writers mocked their law. Christian readers see the light reaching the nations through Christ (John 1:5; 8:12); Jewish readers see it in the Torah itself. The word ἄφθαρτος is the book's word for what does not decay.
orig: τὸ ἄφθαρτον νόμου φῶς (to aphtharton nomou phōs)

a: one child was put out to die and was saved
t: Moses in the basket, and the fitting punishment
p: Pharaoh's order to drown Israel's sons is repaid by the death of Egypt's firstborn and the drowning of its army.
b: Pharaoh ordered, "Every son who is born, you must throw into the Nile" (Exodus 1:22). Moses' mother "laid the child in it and placed it in the reeds by the bank of the Nile" (Exodus 2:3). Wisdom uses the Greek word for exposing an unwanted baby (ἐκτίθημι), a practice its Greek-speaking readers knew well. The writer sees two fitting punishments: Egypt's children die (the firstborn), and those who drowned Israel's babies are themselves drowned "in the mighty water" of the sea. The one rescued child becomes the leader who brings the plagues.

a: Our fathers knew about that night beforehand
p: The "fathers" may be the patriarchs, who were told of the Exodus, or the generation in Egypt, warned of the night.
b: Two readings are common. The patriarchs: God told Abraham that his offspring would be oppressed and that "I will judge the nation they serve, and afterward they will come out with great wealth" (Genesis 15:14), and Wisdom speaks of "oaths" they trusted, which fits the promises to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (18:22). The Israelites in Egypt: Moses told them in advance of the night of the firstborn (Exodus 11:4–7; 12:12–13), so they could "take heart." The Catholic Lectionary reads 18:6–9 on a Sunday with Hebrews 11, which praises Abraham's faith in God's promise.

t: The first Passover as a secret rite
p: Wisdom pictures the first Passover held quietly behind closed doors, with songs already being sung.
b: Exodus 12 has each household kill a lamb and stay inside until morning. Wisdom adds that this was done "in secret" and that the people bound themselves by the "divine law" to share good and bad alike, like a sworn community. It also has "the fathers" leading songs of praise, as Jews later did at the Passover meal, when the Hallel psalms (Psalms 113–118) were sung; the Mishnah records debates on how much of the Hallel to recite there (Mishnah Pesachim 10:6). So the writer reads the Passover of his own day back into the first night.

p: Ἅγιοι here means the members of God's holy people, Israel.
b: Besides ὅσιοι ("holy ones," 18:1), the verse uses ἅγιοι, the word later translated "saints" in the New Testament. Here it means the people bound to one another in the Passover vow, so the Plain says "the holy people." Rendering it "saints" would suggest Christians or canonized holy people, which the writer does not have in view.

p: Israel's songs are answered by Egypt's out-of-tune cry: a musical contrast.
b: The Greek ἀσύμφωνος means "discordant, out of harmony." Against Israel's praise (18:9) comes the Egyptians' wailing for their firstborn, "a great cry" as Exodus 12:30 says. Wisdom likes musical images: the manna was "in tune with every taste" (16:20) and the elements are re-tuned like a harp (19:18). Here two peoples make two kinds of music on the same night.

p: Egypt finally confesses what God had told Pharaoh at the start: Israel is my son.
b: God's first message to Pharaoh was "Israel is my son, my firstborn" (Exodus 4:22), with the warning, "Now I am going to kill your son, your firstborn" (Exodus 4:23). Wisdom says the death of the firstborn forced the Egyptians to admit it. Hosea remembers, "I called my son out of Egypt" (Hosea 11:1), and Matthew 2:15 applies the line to Jesus. In Wisdom 2:13–18 the ungodly mock the righteous man for calling himself God's child; here the whole people is God's son.

a: While still silence lay over everything
p: The Western church sings 18:14–15 at Christmas, of the Word coming down at night.
b: In the older Roman Missal the entrance chant (Introit) for the Sunday within the Octave of Christmas begins Dum medium silentium tenerent omnia: "While all things were in deep silence, and the night was in the middle of its course, your almighty word, O Lord, came down from heaven, from the royal throne" (from 18:14–15). The church applies the verse to the birth of Christ, the Word made flesh, in the silence of night. In Wisdom itself the word comes not to save Egypt but to strike its firstborn; the liturgy reads the image of the word leaving heaven in the light of John 1:14.

t: The all-powerful word, and the Word of John 1
p: Wisdom pictures God's word as a warrior. Christians later read the verse of Christ, the Word.
b: Λόγος is "word," and παντοδύναμος, "all-powerful," occurs in Swete's Greek Bible only in Wisdom (7:23, of Wisdom's spirit; 11:17, of God's hand; and here). In its setting the word is God's command in action, as in "He sent his word to heal them" (Psalm 107:20) and "so will my word be that goes out from my mouth" (Isaiah 55:11). Jewish readers take it as a vivid figure of speech for God himself acting. Christian readers hear John 1:1, "In the beginning was the Word," and Revelation 19:13, where the rider's "name has been called the Word of God." The Plain keeps a small letter, so the text does not decide between these readings.
orig: ὁ παντοδύναμός σου λόγος (ho pantodynamos sou logos)

p: Exodus says the LORD himself struck the firstborn. Wisdom gives the act to his word.
b: Goes beyond: Exodus 12:29 says "In the middle of the night the LORD struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt," and Exodus 12:23 also mentions "the destroyer." Wisdom fills the scene with a single figure, God's word, a warrior with a sword. This keeps God's own hands at a distance while making clear that the act was his. "The LORD is a man of war" (Exodus 15:3) stands behind it. Translators' handbooks note that Wisdom tends to set God's anger apart from God himself, calling it "the punisher" (18:22) and "the destroyer" (18:25).

p: The word carrying a sharp sword links to Isaiah 49, Hebrews 4 and Revelation 19.
b: Isaiah's servant says, "He made my mouth a sharp sword" (Isaiah 49:2). Hebrews says, "The word of God is alive and at work. It cuts deeper than any sword with two edges" (Hebrews 4:12). Revelation's rider, "the Word of God," has a sharp sword from his mouth "to strike the nations with" (Revelation 19:13–15). Wisdom's sword is God's "command, which was no empty threat" (ἀνυπόκριτος, literally "not play-acted"): what God says, he does.

a: It reached to heaven, and yet it had set foot on the earth
p: The giant figure recalls the destroying angel David saw between earth and sky.
b: When God sent a plague on Jerusalem, "David looked up and saw the LORD's angel standing between earth and sky, his sword drawn in his hand" (1 Chronicles 21:16). The Greek of 1 Chronicles 21:15 calls him "the angel who was destroying," with the same root as Wisdom's "destroyer" in 18:25. Wisdom seems to draw on that scene for its picture of the word: sword in hand, filling the space from earth to heaven. Christian readers have also seen here a hint of the Word who is both heavenly and on earth.

p: Exodus says nothing of dreams on the night of the firstborn. Wisdom adds them.
b: Goes beyond: in Wisdom the dying Egyptians are warned in dreams, so each one knows why he dies (18:19). This serves the book's teaching that God's punishments are fair and meant to be understood (11:16; 12:2). The detail has no basis in Exodus 12. It is the writer's own interpretation.

a: a plague broke out on the crowd in the wilderness
p: Verses 20–25 retell Numbers 16:41–50, when Aaron ran into the crowd with incense.
b: After Korah's rebellion the whole community complained, "You have killed the LORD's people!" (Numbers 16:41). A plague began, and Moses told Aaron to take fire and incense and "make atonement for them" (Numbers 16:46). Aaron "ran into the middle of the assembly" and "stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was held back" (Numbers 16:47–48). Wisdom's word for plague, θραῦσις, is the very word of the Greek Numbers. As usual Wisdom names no one, but its readers knew this was Aaron.

t: Prayer and incense as a weapon
p: Aaron fights the plague with priestly weapons: prayer and incense.
b: Numbers 16:47 says Aaron "put on the incense and made atonement for the people." Wisdom adds prayer and calls them his ὅπλον, his weapon. Incense rising with prayer is an old image (Psalm 141:2), and Revelation shows an angel offering incense "to add to the prayers of all the saints" (Revelation 8:3). Christian readers often set Aaron beside Christ the high priest, of whom Hebrews says, "He lives always, to plead for them" (Hebrews 7:25).

p: The Greek ὄχλος usually means "crowd." Translators have made it "the destroyer," "the disturbance" or "the wrath."
b: All the Greek codices that Swete reports read ὄχλον, "crowd, throng," a word that can also mean "trouble, annoyance." The Latin has turbas, "crowds" (Douay "the disturbance"), and the KJV "the destroyer." Some modern translations print "wrath," treating ὄχλον as a copying slip for χόλον, "anger," the same letters in a different order; they mark this as a correction of the Greek. The Plain keeps the Greek and renders it "turmoil," which fits a raging plague. Whichever is right, the point stands: Aaron won with a word, not weapons.

a: by calling to mind the oaths and covenants made with the fathers
p: Numbers records no words from Aaron. Wisdom gives him Moses' kind of prayer.
b: Goes beyond: in Numbers 16 Aaron acts but does not speak. Wisdom says he won "with a word," reminding God of the oaths to the patriarchs. That is the prayer Moses made after the golden calf: "Remember Abraham, Isaac and Israel, your servants. You swore to them by your own self" (Exodus 32:13). Wisdom's Aaron prays in the same way. The point for its readers: God's promises are the strongest argument in prayer.

a: the whole world was on his ankle-length robe
t: The high priest's robe as the universe
p: Wisdom, Philo and Josephus all say the high priest's clothes pictured the whole world.
b: The Greek ποδήρης, "reaching to the feet," is the Septuagint word for the high priest's robe (Exodus 28:4). The "four rows of stones" are the breastpiece with the names of the twelve tribes (Exodus 28:17–21), and the "crown" is the gold plate on the turban, engraved "Holy to the LORD" (Exodus 28:36). Philo of Alexandria says of the robe, "In its whole it is a copy and representation of the world", so that when the high priest enters to pray the whole world enters with him (Life of Moses 2.117, 133). Josephus explains the colors and stones as earth, sky, sun, moon and zodiac (Antiquities 3.179–187). Wisdom shares this Jewish tradition.

p: "The destroyer" is the figure of Exodus 12:23, named again in Hebrews 11 and 1 Corinthians 10.
b: Exodus 12:23 promises that the LORD "will not let the destroyer come into your houses"; the Greek there is τὸν ὀλεθρεύοντα, from the same root as Wisdom's ὁ ὀλοθρεύων. Hebrews 11:28 speaks of "the one who destroyed the firstborn," and Paul warns against grumbling like those who "were destroyed by the Destroyer" (1 Corinthians 10:10), thinking of this same wilderness plague. Whether the destroyer is an angel, God's anger personified, or God himself is debated; Wisdom seems to mean God's anger set to work, which "gave way" when the priest stood in its path.

a: for he knew ahead of time what they would do next
p: Exodus says God hardened Pharaoh's heart. Wisdom stresses foreknowledge and Egypt's own folly.
b: Exodus says, "I will make Pharaoh's heart stubborn, and he will chase after them" (Exodus 14:4). Wisdom puts it differently: God knew in advance that they would change their minds, and "the fate they deserved dragged them" (19:4). Readers have long debated how God's hardening and human choice fit together. Wisdom's way of telling it puts the weight on Egypt's guilt and God's foreknowledge; readers who stress God's sovereign choice point instead to Paul's use of the Pharaoh story in Romans 9:17–18. Wisdom does not settle that debate, but it shows how one Jewish writer read Exodus 14.

p: The Greek ἀνάγκη, "necessity," was the Greek word for fate. Wisdom makes it moral.
b: In Greek thought ἀνάγκη was the blind force of fate that even the gods obey. Wisdom calls it ἀξία ἀνάγκη, a "deserved necessity": not blind fate, but the consequence of guilt, under God's control. The Egyptians are drawn to the sea by the logic of their own sin, so that they "fill up" the measure of punishment. Compare Genesis 15:16, "the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full," and 1 Thessalonians 2:16.
orig: ἡ ἀξία ... ἀνάγκη (hē axia ... anankē), 'the deserved necessity'

a: was shaped again from the start
p: At the sea, Wisdom says, creation was refashioned, each kind from the beginning.
b: The verb διατυπόω means to shape or mold, and ἄνωθεν means "anew, from the start" (the same word as "born from above" in John 3:3). "In its own kind" (ἐν ἰδίῳ γένει) recalls Genesis 1, where each creature is made "by its kind" (Genesis 1:21, 24). So the crossing of the sea is a second creation: dry land rises out of water (19:7), as on the third day. The thought prepares 19:18–21, where the elements change roles. Christian readers link it with Paul's "new creation" (2 Corinthians 5:17) and with creation set free from decay (Romans 8:21).

t: Red Sea or Sea of Reeds
p: The Greek says "the Red Sea"; the Hebrew name is Yam Suf, "Sea of Reeds."
b: Wisdom writes in Greek and uses the Septuagint's name, ἐρυθρὰ θάλασσα, "the Red Sea" (as in the Greek of Psalm 105:9 and Exodus 15:4). The Hebrew of Exodus calls it Yam Suf, which this site renders "Sea of Reeds" in the books translated from Hebrew. Where the crossing took place is debated; see the topic page. The Plain of Wisdom keeps the Greek name because that is what the book says.

p: Exodus says the Israelites walked on dry ground. Wisdom pictures a grassy plain.
b: Goes beyond: Exodus says the LORD "turned the sea into dry ground" (Exodus 14:21) and the Israelites walked "on dry ground, with the water standing as a wall" (Exodus 14:22). Wisdom imagines more: a green meadow where the waves had been, with Israel grazing "like horses at pasture" (19:9). The image may grow from Isaiah 63:13, where God led them through the deeps "like a horse in the wilderness," and Psalm 106:9, "he walked them through the deeps as though it were the wilderness." It belongs to the new-creation theme of 19:6.

a: They roamed like horses at pasture, and they skipped like lambs
p: The picture draws on Isaiah 63 and Psalm 114, the songs of the Exodus.
b: Isaiah 63:13 remembers the crossing: "Like a horse in the wilderness, / they did not stumble." Psalm 114, a Hallel psalm about the Exodus, has "The mountains leapt like rams, / the hills like young sheep" (Psalm 114:4). Wisdom moves the leaping from the hills to the people themselves. The scene is pure joy, and it ends in praise of the Lord "their rescuer," as Exodus 15 ends the crossing with Moses' song.

p: In Egypt the land made gnats and the river made frogs: the order of Genesis 1 turned upside down.
b: In Genesis 1 the land brings out living creatures "by its kind" (Genesis 1:24) and the waters swarm with water creatures (Genesis 1:20–21). In the plagues the dust of the ground "turned to gnats" (Exodus 8:17) and the Nile swarmed with frogs that came up onto the land (Exodus 8:3). Wisdom notices the reversal: instead of cattle, gnats; instead of fish, frogs. Then in the wilderness came a new kind of birth for birds, the quail from the sea (19:11–12). The plagues undo creation for Egypt; the Exodus remakes it for Israel.

p: Wisdom turns a common Greek charge against Jews back on the Egyptians.
b: The Greek μισοξενία, "hatred of strangers," occurs nowhere else in Swete's Greek Old Testament. Greek and Egyptian critics of the Jews in Alexandria accused them of hating outsiders. Josephus answers one of them, Apion, who claimed that Jews swore by God "to bear no good will to any foreigner" (Against Apion 2.121). Wisdom replies in advance: it was Egypt that welcomed Jacob's family and then enslaved them, a worse hatred of strangers than even Sodom's (19:14). For readers in Alexandria the point was close to home.

a: Others refused to take in strangers they did not know
p: "Others" are the men of Sodom. The Greek does not name them; the KJV adds "the Sodomites."
b: Verses 13–17 compare Egypt with Sodom, as the next verses make clear (19:17 recalls the blindness at Lot's door, Genesis 19:11). The Greek says only "those"; the KJV's "the Sodomites" is an explanation, not in the Greek. Wisdom judges Sodom's sin as inhospitality to strangers, as Ezekiel 16:49 judges it as pride and neglect of the poor; Jude 1:7 speaks of sexual immorality. Egypt, Wisdom says, was worse: Sodom rejected strangers it did not know, but Egypt enslaved guests who had helped it, Joseph above all.

a: there will surely be a visitation for those others
t: A hard verse: judgment or leniency for Sodom?
p: The Greek can mean that Sodom will be judged, or that Sodom will get some consideration.
b: The Greek ἀλλ᾽ ἦ τις ἐπισκοπὴ ἔσται αὐτῶν is unclear. Ἐπισκοπή, "visitation," can mean God's coming to judge (as in 14:11) or to show favor (as in 3:7). Judgment: Sodom will surely be punished for its hostility to strangers, and Egypt deserves worse. Leniency: the KJV has "peradventure some respect shall be had of those," that is, Sodom will get some allowance because it only received strangers coldly. The Latin goes its own way: the others received strangers "against their will." The Plain keeps the neutral word "visitation."
orig: ἦ τις ἐπισκοπὴ ἔσται αὐτῶν (ē tis episkopē estai autōn)

p: Egypt welcomed Jacob's family with a feast and then made them slaves.
b: Pharaoh told Joseph, "Settle your father and brothers in the best of the land" (Genesis 47:6), but a later king put "slave-gang bosses over them" (Exodus 1:11). Wisdom calls the Israelites people who "already shared the same rights," using δίκαια, a legal word for civic rights. Jews in Alexandria lived under Greek and then Roman rule with a disputed standing in the city, and in AD 38 they suffered riots that Philo describes in Against Flaccus. Many readers hear in this verse a protest from that setting, whatever the exact date of the book.
orig: τῶν αὐτῶν μετεσχηκότας δικαίων (tōn autōn meteschēkotas dikaiōn)

a: They were struck with blindness too
p: Wisdom uses the rare word of Genesis 19:11 for the blindness at Lot's door.
b: At Sodom the angels "struck the men at the doorway of the house ... with blindness, so that they wore themselves out trying to find the door" (Genesis 19:11). The Greek there has ἀορασία, the same rare word Wisdom uses; in Swete's Greek Old Testament it occurs only five times. Wisdom applies it to the darkness of Egypt (Exodus 10:23), when each person "groped for the way through his own door." Lot is "the righteous man," as in 10:6 and 2 Peter 2:7.

p: Στοιχεῖα are the basic elements of the world: earth, water, air and fire.
b: Greek science counted four elements, and Solomon has already said that God taught him "how the elements work" (7:17). Here it explains the miracles of the Exodus: the elements did not stop being themselves, but changed their roles, as notes on a harp keep their sounds while the tune changes. Land creatures went through water (Israel and its flocks), water creatures came on land (the frogs), fire burned in water (the hail), and fire spared ice (the manna). Paul uses the same word for the "elements" or "basic principles" of the world (Galatians 4:3; Colossians 2:8).

a: the way notes on a harp change what the melody is called
p: Changing the tuning of a harp makes a new mode from the same strings.
b: Greek music named its scales or modes (Dorian, Lydian and others). Retune a few strings and the same harp plays in a new mode, though every string keeps its own kind of sound. Wisdom uses this to say that miracles do not break nature but re-tune it: God plays a different tune on the same creation. The image completes the book's musical language (16:20, 24; 18:9–10).
orig: ὥσπερ ἐν ψαλτηρίῳ φθόγγοι τοῦ ῥυθμοῦ τὸ ὄνομα διαλλάσσουσιν

a: Creatures of dry land became creatures of the water
t: Land animals in the sea, swimmers on land
p: Israel's flocks walked through the sea; the frogs came up on land.
b: The two lines sum up the Exodus as an exchange of places. Israel's cattle and sheep, land animals, went through the middle of the sea (Exodus 14:22; 12:38). Frogs, water creatures, came up out of the Nile into Egypt's houses (Exodus 8:3). To the writer this shows the elements "re-tuned" (19:18).

p: Wisdom calls the manna by the Greek name for the food of the gods.
b: In Greek myth, from Homer on, ambrosia was the food that kept the gods immortal. Wisdom borrows the word for the manna, which it has already called "the food of angels" (16:20). A reader of Vaticanus added a note in the margin, "divine," to explain the word. Verdict: the writer is not adopting Greek religion. He takes the most glorious food word in Greek and gives it to the true God's gift, telling Greek-speaking readers that Israel ate what the poets only dreamed of. In Swete's Greek Old Testament the word appears only here.

a: at every time and in every place
p: The book ends with one line of praise, with no return to Solomon and no closing prayer.
b: After the long comparison of Egypt and Israel, the book simply ends: God has made his people great and stood by them always. The ending is sudden. It can be read as unfinished, or as a deliberate summary of chapters 10–19, the story of God's care in history, and turns it into a promise for the writer's own day: as at the sea, so in Alexandria. Christians read "every time and every place" as a promise to God's people in every age.
